restate.summary:
The document builds a theory of what a claim is and how to analyze one, in three stages: a grounding ladder, a set of derived definitions, and seven analysis pipelines.

STAGE 1 — THE ANTI-CIRCULARITY MOVE. The author's foundational worry is circularity: if every claim is justified by other claims, nothing is ever grounded. The escape is what the author calls the "law of non-circularity," an observed regularity that every cycle originates from something that is not itself a member of the cycle (chickens from a non-chicken, life from non-life, universe from non-universe; and in logic: deductions from inductions, inductions from observations, observations from phenomena). Applied to claims, this means all chains of claims must terminate in something that is not a claim. The candidates are phenomena — raw occurrences like "red," "anger," "2" — which are the ultimate givens: they simply occur, they are not asserted, so they cannot be circularly justified. Everything else in the framework is built on top of them.

STAGE 2 — THE DEFINITION LADDER. Definitions are stacked so that each new concept is either a directly observable feature of phenomena or an earlier concept restricted to a narrower "context." The ladder: (1) phenomena occur; (2) phenomena are distinct from one another (differences occur); (3) phenomena carry qualities, where associations between phenomena are themselves a kind of quality; (4) among the qualities we find will, temporal qualia (before/after/time), and "scope," defined as a pattern that a set of observations share; (5) correlation = one phenomenon often follows another; (6) independence = no correlation, and necessity = correlation without exception. Then the context-restriction moves begin: (7) "ontological" = whatever is independent of will (the author includes will itself and unobserved things under this heading); (8) causality = necessity, restricted to the context of ontological events — and by the non-circularity law, causal chains must start at an uncaused event; (9) intellectual causality = causality, restricted to the context of imagination/thought — and intellectual chains must start at something non-intellectual, i.e., a phenomenological primitive; (10) truth = intellectual causality, restricted to the context of undeniability (with the caveat that truth is context/domain-relative, the way Newtonian mechanics is true within its domain even though relativity exists); (11) a claim = a statement with a truth-value. A parallel cluster of definitions fills in the machinery: a statement is an inferential structure (equivalently, a set of definitions plus their associations); an event is an ontic structure; a truth-value is whether the inferential structure corresponds to the ontic structure it refers to (truth = it corresponds, falsehood = it doesn't); faithfulness is the analogous correspondence for communicative structures; a proof is a sequence of claims in an inferential structure; a conclusion is a proof's final step; a proof is "grounded" when its first step is phenomenological, "valid" when the conclusion's link to prior steps occurs by intellectual causality, and "sound" when every link does. Deniability — the hinge of the truth definition — means: given what you currently know, does denying the thing produce an inconsistency? This is an internal, phenomenological event (a felt "knowing you're wrong"), not public disavowal. Falsehood is intellectual causality within the context of deniability. The author stresses that undeniability still operates in probabilistic domains: for "there is microbial life outside Earth," you don't demand direct observation (that would be hyperskepticism); you apply abductive reasoning layer by layer — statistical inference, universal physics, atmospheric chemistry — and undeniability is assessed at each scope layer, down to the claim.

STAGE 3 — THE SEVEN PIPELINES. A claim's full structure decomposes into seven analyses, each shaped the same way: start at the claim, walk backward through a repeating "cycle" of intermediate elements, and terminate at a non-circular ground. (1) MEANING — "what does the claim say?" Unpack each definition into the definitions it depends on, until you bottom out in phenomenological primitives. Output: what the claim is talking about — what to imagine. ("Definition" here covers anything that references something specific: concepts, terms, etc.) (2) SCOPE/REFERENCE — "what is the claim about; what scope does it live under?" Trace the claim's scope through cycles of definition-scopes and pattern identification down to primitives (a scope being, phenomenologically, a pattern that joins/categorizes observations). Output: the part of reality under discussion. (3) ONTOLOGY — "what has to happen in reality for this claim to occur?" Take the ontological event the claim refers to and trace its causes back through the causal cycle to an intrinsic cause, with "cause" operating inside the scope established in pipeline 2. Output: how the claim fits the known ontological conditions for it. (4) PROOF — "what justifies/points to the claim?" A chain of signs/supports, each pointing to the next, bottoming out in phenomenological primitives. Signs merely point (I feel wet; I see rain; the droplets correspond to the feeling) — the licensing logic is handled separately. Output: the claim's external justification, observable by anyone. (5) INFERENTIAL — "what allows the proof to lead to the claim?" The rules of inference connecting the signs to the claim, grounded ultimately in logical/intellectual causality. Output: the claim's internal/logical justification. (6) TRUTH — "what makes the claim true?" Apply the deniability test to the outputs of all the prior pipelines — meaning, scope, proof, inferential proof, and the known ontological conditions. Output: the claim's truth-value. (7) COMMUNICATION — "how to faithfully communicate the claim?" Choose and shape wording ("demystification") according to the audience's knowledge, disposition, and language, which are in turn grounded in human psychological nature. Output: a proper, faithful understanding of the claim in the audience. (The author marks this pipeline as tentative.)

SUPPORTING DOCTRINES. Statements have two graded properties: comprehensibility (is it imaginable at all, regardless of observed context — "pink elephants" are imaginable; positive form coherence, negative incoherence; bounded by the limits of imagination) and rationality (are the definitions comprehensible within their real contexts — a pink elephant is irrational because elephants aren't pink; bounded by the precedent of reality, and revisable by the "refinement" step of the scientific method). The structure of a claim itself bears on its truth: a justification that would equally confirm a falsehood — like a clock whose hands point to all times, or a smoke detector that beeps with no smoke — cannot establish truth; so one condition for truth is that the proof structure can distinguish truth from falsehood (including truth mixed with falsehood). Since a claim's parts and their connections are themselves claims with their own structures, there may be a self-referential/recursive component to claims. Reason is defined as a sequence of intellectual causality — something discovered, not decided — and the scientific method (Observation → Definition → Induction → Deduction → Refinement) is glossed as: grounding in reality → something identifiable with clear scope → identifying the pattern behind the defined scopes → applying observational precedent → refining scopes with new information. The author also argues at length that the modern "neutral default" (agnostic, physicalist, hyperskeptical) is not actually neutral: it has rivals, it has its own hard problems (intrinsic nature of causality, energy, etc.), hard problems are merely synonyms for limits of knowledge (all knowledge is domain-relative), "speculation as proof/refutation" is another all-pointing clock, and the illusion-vs-reality skeptical puzzle dissolves once you note that "reality" was originally defined as whatever is independent of will — so illusions and dreams are categorizations *within* reality, and the puzzle came from semantically drifting the word "real."

The document closes with two compressed "phenomenological reductions": truth = a necessary, ontological (non-willed) event that is an undeniable imagination; and a claim = an undeniable set of definitions and their associations (a false claim being a deniable one), referring to a necessary ontological event, where the ontological event correlates with the intellectual event.

guesses: Reconciling the three characterizations of truth: the ladder says truth = intellectual causality within the context of undeniability; item 12.3 says truth = correspondence between inferential and ontic structure; the closing reduction says truth = a necessary ontological event that is an undeniable imagination. The document never states how these relate. I guessed they are intended as the same notion expressed at different levels of reduction, but the text underdetermines this.

The parenthetical in the 'ontological' definition — 'independent of will (including will itself, as well as whatever is not directly observed)'. I read it as: will itself counts as ontological (it occurs whether or not you will it), and unobserved things also count. But the grammar allows other readings (e.g., that 'independent of will' must be understood as also excluding will), and the text does not disambiguate.

In rung 9, 'intellectual events are caused by others [in which all the above are ontological, even your own will]' — what 'all the above' refers to is unclear. I guessed it means the causes of intellectual events are themselves ontological events (including one's own will), consistent with rung 7, but this is a guess.

The arrow/bracket notation of the Truth pipeline: 'claim (its truth-value) <- deniability (known ontological conditions) & (deniability [inferential proof] <- deniability [proof]) <- deniability (scope) <- deniability (meaning)'. The exact dependency ordering — what feeds what, and whether the '&' branches run in parallel — is underdetermined. I guessed it means: apply the deniability test to each prior pipeline's output, layered from meaning up through scope, proof, inferential proof, and ontological conditions.

The '...' in the Scope pipeline's 'cycle of (definition scope <- pattern identification <- ...)' leaves the cycle's continuation unspecified. I guessed it alternates definition-scope and pattern-identification steps until reaching phenomenological primitives.

'Intrinsic cause' (terminus of the Ontology pipeline) is never defined. By parallel with rung 8's 'uncaused event' and the non-circularity law, I guessed it means the uncaused first cause terminating the causal chain within the relevant scope — but equating 'intrinsic cause' with 'uncaused event' is my inference, not the document's statement.

The Communication pipeline ends with a '?', and 'demystification' is only glossed as '(word choice, selection, etc.)'. I guessed demystification means selecting wording that removes obscurity for the specific audience; the author marks the whole pipeline as tentative, so its details are underdetermined by design.

'Communicative structure' (in the definition of faithfulness) is never defined. I guessed it means the linguistic/expressed form of a claim (spoken, written, etc.), parallel to inferential and ontic structures.

The closing reduction defines a claim as 'an undeniable set of definitions and their associations,' while rung 11 defines a claim as a statement with a truth-value (which may be false). Since the reduction adds 'a false claim would be a deniable one,' I guessed the reduction is describing the fully successful (true) claim, with the deniable variant covering falsehood — but the text does not explicitly resolve the tension.

The deniability definition itself carries a question mark ('...results in an inconsistency/knowing you're wrong?') and refers to 'as explained earlier,' but the earlier explanation is not in this document. I took the internal-inconsistency reading (supported by the microbial-life example), but the author's own phrasing is tentative.

In Note 5, the mapping of Deduction — 'Apply observational precedent to patterns? and/or, observe what occurs after intellectual causality occurs?' — contains the author's own question marks. I preserved both alternatives rather than choosing; the intended reading is underdetermined. Likewise 'Reason (proof?)' leaves open whether reason and proof are identical.

Whether the seven pipelines are strictly ordered (each consuming the previous one's output) is only partially stated: pipeline 3 says 'cause' operates within the scope defined earlier, and pipeline 6 consumes all previous outputs. I guessed the listed order (meaning → scope → ontology → proof → inferential → truth → communication) reflects an intended dependency ordering throughout, but the document only establishes it for those two cases.

Why will, temporal qualia, and scope all appear together at rung 4 of the ladder, and what ordering principle places them there, is not explained; I treated rung placement as roughly 'what each concept presupposes' without textual confirmation.

In Note 4 the author explicitly leaves open whether 'truth from the structure of a claim' is just the claim's self-referential nature 'or perhaps something more - idk.' I reported the uncertainty rather than resolving it; any firmer reading would be a guess.
In the abduction discussion, the 'metric X' by which one prefers hypothesis A over B is deliberately left unspecified ('by some metric X'); I did not assign it a specific meaning.

apply.decomposition:
Reading convention I adopted: the document writes every pipeline as "claim <- ... <- phenomenological primitive(s)", where "<-" means "is grounded in." To RUN a pipeline I therefore build from the rightmost term (the primitive) leftward until I arrive at the claim. Claim under analysis: "Aspirin reduces fever."

=== PIPELINE 1 — MEANING ===
Arrow: claim (the 'what') <- cycle of (definition <- definition) <- phenomenological primitive. ("definition" = concepts/terms/anything referencing something specific.)
Trace (right -> left):
- Primitive base: levels 1-4 of the ladder — "phenomena occur," "distinct phenomena occur," "qualities & associations occur," "temporal qualia occur."
- Cycle of definitions, one term at a time:
  - "fever" := the quality body-heat (level 3, quality) at a degree distinct (level 2, difference) from ordinary body-heat. Bottoms out at the warmth-quale under "qualities occur."
  - "aspirin" := a distinct phenomenon (level 2) — one specific substance/pill — individuated by its qualities & associations (level 3). Bottoms out at "distinct phenomena occur."
  - "reduces" := a temporal-comparative relation — the fever-quality is greater "before" and lesser "after" (level 4, temporal qualia). Bottoms out at "temporal qualia occur."
- Assemble leftward into the claim: a distinct substance (aspirin) associated with the body-heat quality decreasing across time.
OUTPUT (what the claim is talking about / what to imagine): Imagine a distinct substance called aspirin entering a body that carries the felt/observed quality of excess heat (fever), and imagine that heat-quality being greater at an earlier moment and lesser at a later moment — the picture of a hot, feverish body cooling after the substance is taken.

=== PIPELINE 2 — SCOPE / REFERENCE ===
Arrow: claim (its scope) <- cycle of (definition scope <- pattern identification <- ...) <- phenomenological primitives. (A scope is "a pattern that a set of observations have," level 4.)
Trace (right -> left):
- Primitives: many distinct observations of bodies, substances, temperatures.
- Pattern identification: across these observations, "a body given aspirin" is often followed by "that body's heat-quality dropping" (correlation, level 5). That recurring pattern IS the scope-pattern.
- Definition scope: categorize the pattern as the domain of febrile bodies + ingested substances (physiological/pharmacological events), held as a scope of tendency/probability rather than single-case certainty — following the document's own microbial-life note that undeniability can live at the statistical level.
OUTPUT (the part of reality we're talking about): The pharmacological/physiological scope — the categorized set of observations of fever-bearing bodies that ingest aspirin. The part of reality is that population/domain of body-plus-aspirin events, framed as a statistical tendency.

=== PIPELINE 3 — ONTOLOGY ===
Arrow: claim (its known ontological conditions) <- ontological event (that it references) <- cycle of (cause <- cause) <- intrinsic cause. ("cause" occurs within the scope from Pipeline 2; ontological = not-willed; causality = necessity within ontological events.)
Trace (right -> left):
- Intrinsic cause: per the law of non-circularity, the causal cycle must start from an uncaused/intrinsic cause within the pharmacological scope — the point where tracing exits the scope (the intrinsic chemical nature of the aspirin substance and the body's intrinsic thermoregulatory nature). [Flagged — see stuck points.]
- Cycle of cause <- cause (within scope): aspirin ingested <- aspirin present in the body <- aspirin acting on the fever-raising mechanism (necessity: holds without exception within scope) <- body's heat-setpoint lowered <- measured body-heat decreases.
- Ontological event referenced: the not-willed event of a body's fever actually decreasing after aspirin.
OUTPUT (a fit with the known ontological conditions): The claim FITS — its referenced not-willed event (fever decreasing) is reachable by a chain of causes-within-scope from aspirin ingestion down to the measured decrease, terminating (per non-circularity) in an intrinsic cause. The claim is consistent with the known ontological conditions for a substance lowering body-heat.

=== PIPELINE 4 — PROOF ===
Arrow: claim (proof) <- cycle of (sign/support <- sign/support) <- phenomenological primitives. (Signs "point to" the claim; the logic connecting them is Pipeline 5.)
Trace (right -> left):
- Primitives: the actual felt/seen observations.
- Cycle of signs/supports: sign — a thermometer reading is lower after aspirin than before (observable by anyone); support — that drop recurs across many feverish bodies given aspirin, and recurs more than when nothing is given. Each sign points at the claim the way "seeing rain" pointed at "I am wet" in the document's example.
OUTPUT (external justification, for anyone to observe for themselves): The observable, repeatable signs — measured body-temperature falls after aspirin is administered, recurring across many cases (and more than without it). Anyone can give aspirin to a feverish body, watch the thermometer, and observe the sign directly.

=== PIPELINE 5 — INFERENTIAL ===
Arrow: claim <- inferences <- cycle of (rule of inference <- rule of inference) <- logical/intellectual causality.
Trace (right -> left):
- Base: intellectual causality (level 9) — the links are discovered, not decided.
- Cycle of rules of inference: correlation (level 5: fever-drop often follows aspirin) <- if it holds without exception, necessity (level 6) <- within not-willed events this necessity is causality (level 8: aspirin causes the drop) <- inductive generalization from the recurring sign to the general claim <- abduction (best explanation of the recurring sign is that aspirin reduces fever).
- Inferences: these rules carry the Pipeline-4 signs up to the claim.
OUTPUT (internal/logical justification): The rules of inference that make the signs actually lead to the claim — correlation upgraded to necessity/causality within not-willed events, plus inductive generalization and abduction — grounded in intellectual causality. This is what stops the proof from being a bare coincidence.

=== PIPELINE 6 — TRUTH ===
Arrow: claim (its truth-value) <- deniability (known ontological conditions) & (deniability [inferential proof] <- deniability [proof]) <- deniability (scope) <- deniability (meaning). (Deniability = does denying it produce inconsistency/knowing-you're-wrong; truth = undeniable, falsehood = deniable.) I read the "&"/nesting as: apply the deniability test to every prior output and conjoin — the claim is true iff each is undeniable.
Trace (applying deniability to each earlier output):
- Deniability(meaning): denying that the claim coherently pictures aspirin/fever/decrease is inconsistent — the meaning is coherent and rational. UNDENIABLE.
- Deniability(scope): denying that the claim belongs to the pharmacological/statistical scope is inconsistent. UNDENIABLE.
- Deniability(proof): denying the observed recurring temperature-drop sign contradicts observation. UNDENIABLE (at the statistical level, per the microbial-life caveat).
- Deniability(inferential proof): denying the correlation->causality/induction link while accepting the signs is inconsistent. UNDENIABLE. (And the proof distinguishes truth from falsehood — it is NOT a "clock whose hands point at all times," because the drop tracks aspirin specifically rather than confirming any outcome.)
- Deniability(known ontological conditions): denying the causal fit contradicts the Pipeline-3 output. UNDENIABLE.
- Conjoin (&): all prior outputs are undeniable.
OUTPUT (the claim's truth-value): TRUE — within the pharmacological scope and at the level of statistical/probabilistic undeniability, denying "aspirin reduces fever" produces inconsistency with the meaning, scope, proof, inferential proof, and ontological conditions. It would come out FALSE only if some link were deniable.

=== PIPELINE 7 — COMMUNICATION ===
Arrow: claim (communication) <- demystification (word choice, selection, etc.) <- audience knowledge & audience disposition & audience language <- (human) psychological nature. (Faithfulness = the communicative structure corresponds to the inferential/ontic structures it refers to.)
Trace (right -> left):
- (Human) psychological nature: how a mind receives words. [Document marks this grounding with a "?" — uncertain.]
- Audience knowledge & disposition & language: e.g., layperson vs. clinician; their prior vocabulary; their trust/skepticism.
- Demystification / word choice: pick words so the received picture matches the ontic/inferential structure fixed by the earlier pipelines. Layperson: "Taking aspirin usually brings a fever down" (conveys tendency, not a guaranteed cure, not "always"). Clinician: specify dose, mechanism, and that "reduces" is not "eliminates."
OUTPUT (a proper, faithful understanding of the claim): A rendering whose words make the audience imagine exactly the probabilistic, causal fever-lowering the earlier pipelines established — no more ("aspirin always cures fever") and no less — tuned to that audience's knowledge, disposition, and language, so the communicative structure faithfully corresponds to the inferential/ontic structures.
stuck_points: Arrow direction / entry point: the document never states whether a pipeline is 'run' right-to-left or left-to-right. The '<-' is only defined implicitly as grounding. I improvised by reading '<-' as 'is grounded in' and building each pipeline from the rightmost phenomenological primitive up to the claim.

Cycle termination: every pipeline contains a 'cycle of (X <- X)' with no stated stopping rule beyond eventually reaching a phenomenological primitive (and the non-circularity law that a cycle starts from a non-thing). I improvised by stopping each cycle the moment a term bottomed out at a listed ladder level (e.g., a quality, a distinct phenomenon, a temporal qualia).

Meaning pipeline gives no rule for splitting a multi-word claim into its definitions. I improvised by decomposing into the three lexical terms — 'aspirin', 'reduces', 'fever' — and grounding each separately.

Ontology's 'intrinsic cause': the document asserts the causal cycle 'starts with an uncaused/intrinsic cause' but gives no method to identify it for a concrete claim. I improvised by naming the intrinsic cause as the point where causal tracing exits the pharmacological scope (aspirin's intrinsic chemistry / the body's intrinsic thermoregulation) and flagged it as indeterminate.

Scope pipeline literally leaves the chain open with '...': 'definition scope <- pattern identification <- ...'. I improvised the missing middle by treating pattern identification (correlation across observations) as feeding directly into the scope categorization.

Whether I may import real empirical knowledge of aspirin at all: the instruction says treat the document as the SOLE authority on term meanings, but Pipelines 3-5 require actual causes, signs, and observations about aspirin that the document does not contain. I improvised by importing only minimal empirical content (fever measurably drops after aspirin, recurring across cases) as the raw 'observations/signs/causes' the framework's structure is meant to be filled with, since the framework supplies structure but no pharmacological content.

Ontology depth / 'known ontological conditions' is undefined as to how far down the causal chain must go or what counts as 'known.' I improvised with a short common-knowledge causal chain (ingested -> present -> acts on fever mechanism -> setpoint lowered -> temperature drops) rather than a specific biochemical depth.

Truth pipeline's arrow-structure mixes '&', '<-', and nesting — 'deniability(known ontological conditions) & (deniability[inferential proof] <- deniability[proof]) <- deniability(scope) <- deniability(meaning)' — with no stated rule for how these combine into one truth-value. I improvised by treating it as: apply the deniability test to every prior output and conjoin them ('&' = logical AND), so the claim is true iff each prior output is undeniable.

Truth threshold for statistical/probabilistic undeniability: the microbial-life note says undeniability can operate at the statistical level, but no threshold is given for when statistical undeniability counts as 'true.' I improvised by declaring the claim 'true within scope at the level of statistical undeniability' without any numeric cutoff.

Communication's final grounding is written by the author with a trailing '?' ('(human) psychological nature'?), signaling the author's own uncertainty about the primitive. I improvised by treating human psychological nature as the grounding primitive anyway.

Separating Proof (signs) from Inferential (rules of inference): for this claim the observable sign (temperature drops after aspirin) and the inference (correlation->causality->induction) are entangled, and the document does not say how to cleanly split them. I improvised by assigning the bare observable event to Proof and all the correlation/causality/induction/abduction logic to Inferential.

Output form of the Ontology pipeline: the document says its output is 'a fit with the known ontological conditions,' not a truth-value, so ontology apparently does not itself decide truth. I improvised by rendering 'a fit' as a consistency verdict ('the claim's causal story is consistent with known ontology') rather than as a proof or a true/false judgment.

Primitive singular vs. plural: the Meaning pipeline says 'phenomenological primitive' (singular) while others say 'primitives' (plural), with no explained distinction. I treated both as 'the base phenomenological givens' and did not attach significance to the number.

ambiguities.quote: therefore they fit the induction that all cycles must originate from something that isn't the thing itself
ambiguities.issue: This induction (later named 'the law of non-circularity') is used at the very top of the document to justify starting at phenomenological grounding, yet note 3 says 'Along the way of discovering reality, we somehow discover the law of non-circularity' — i.e., it is discovered downstream of the ladder it is used to found. Its status in the framework's own vocabulary (phenomenological given? correlation? necessity?) and its position on the ladder are never stated, even though rungs 8 and 9 both lean on it.
ambiguities.question_for_author: Where does the law of non-circularity sit on the grounding ladder, and in your own terms is it a phenomenological given, a correlation, or a necessity — given that it both justifies the ladder's starting point and is described as discovered later 'along the way'?

ambiguities.quote: that cycle ends/starts at this stage as phenomena make up of all things if that makes sense
ambiguities.issue: The sentence is grammatically garbled. 'Phenomena make up of all things' could mean 'phenomena constitute all things', 'all things are made up of phenomena', or 'all things are only accessible to us via phenomena' — and each reading changes what 'grounded in something phenomenological' requires. It is also unclear which cycle 'ends/starts' here.
ambiguities.question_for_author: Can you restate this sentence — do you mean everything is composed of phenomena, or everything is only present to us through phenomena — and which cycle is it that 'ends/starts' at this stage?

ambiguities.quote: the cycle starts with a non-intellectual event [ie. phenomenological primitive]
ambiguities.issue: 'Phenomenological primitive' is the terminus of the meaning, scope, and proof pipelines, but is never defined. It is unclear which ladder items count as primitives: only rung-1 raw phenomena and rung-2 distinctions, or also qualities, associations, will, temporal qualia, correlations, etc. Without a criterion, one cannot tell when a grounding chain has legitimately bottomed out.
ambiguities.question_for_author: Exactly which items count as 'phenomenological primitives' — only bare phenomena/distinctions, or everything up to some specific rung — and how do I recognize that a chain has actually reached one?

ambiguities.quote: qualities & associations occur (where associations are a type of quality)
ambiguities.issue: 'Association' is never defined, yet it is load-bearing: note 2 defines a statement as 'a set of definitions + their associations'. It is unclear what distinguishes an association from any other quality, and whether the rung-3 phenomenal sense (something that 'occurs') is the same 'association' that structurally combines definitions inside a statement.
ambiguities.question_for_author: What is an 'association' — how do I tell one apart from other qualities, and is the rung-3 phenomenal sense the same 'association' that combines with definitions to form a statement?

ambiguities.quote: scope is a pattern that a set of observations have
ambiguities.issue: 'Observation' first appears here with no ladder definition, and note 3 later treats observations as derived from phenomena ('observations from phenomena'), implying they are a distinct, unlisted rung. 'Pattern' is also undefined. Since the entire scope pipeline is built on 'pattern' over 'observations', both need fixing before the pipeline can be applied.
ambiguities.question_for_author: What is an 'observation' as distinct from a phenomenon, and where do 'observation' and 'pattern' fall on the ladder relative to rungs 1-4?

ambiguities.quote: correlation is a when a phenomena often follows another
ambiguities.issue: 'Often' has no threshold, and 'follows' restricts correlation to temporal succession — it is unclear whether simultaneous co-occurrence counts as correlation at all. Since necessity, causality, and ultimately truth are all built on this definition, the vagueness propagates upward.
ambiguities.question_for_author: How often is 'often', and does correlation cover only one phenomenon following another in time, or also phenomena that occur together simultaneously?

ambiguities.quote: independence is when phenomena do not correlate
ambiguities.issue: If correlation requires 'often' following, then phenomena that occasionally-but-not-often follow one another appear to be neither correlated nor independent, leaving an unclassified middle category; alternatively 'do not correlate' may mean 'never follow one another'. The document does not say which.

terms.doc_sense: The bottom rung of the grounding ladder: raw givens ('phenomena occur') that are non-claims and therefore terminate every chain of definition, proof, or causation. 'Phenomena make up all things.' A 'phenomenological primitive' is any such given (red, anger, 2, feeling wet) that a chain bottoms out in.
terms.standard_sense: 'Phenomenological' evokes Husserlian phenomenology (a method for analyzing structures of conscious experience) or, in science, a descriptive model without mechanism. 'Phenomenological primitive' is an established term in physics education (diSessa's p-prims: intuitive knowledge fragments). 'Phenomena' are often contrasted with things-in-themselves.
terms.misread_risk: Moderate-high. A philosophy reader will look for Husserlian machinery (epoché, intentionality) that isn't there; the doc uses the word purely for 'the pre-claim given that stops regress.' A physics-education reader would badly misparse 'phenomenological primitive.' Since this term anchors the entire ladder, importing either standard sense skews everything above it.

terms.doc_sense: Any distinguishable aspect that occurs among phenomena — explicitly including associations, will, and 'temporal qualia' ('before', 'after', 'time') as types of quality.
terms.standard_sense: A property or attribute possessed by an object (redness, mass). Will is standardly a faculty, an association a relation, and 'qualia' are the subjective sensory characters of experience — none are 'qualities' in this classificatory sense.
terms.misread_risk: Moderate. A reader treating qualities as static attributes of objects misses that the ladder classifies will and time-experience as occurring qualities — a classification the later definitions ('ontological = not willed', causality's temporal ordering) directly depend on.

terms.doc_sense: 'A pattern that a set of observations have' / a pattern that joins or categorizes observations. Functions as the domain or context a claim lives under (the Newtonian-mechanics example), with claims having scope layers (statistical level, physics level, etc.).
terms.standard_sense: In logic, the reach of a quantifier or operator within a formula. In everyday and project speech, the extent or range of what is covered.
terms.misread_risk: High. Scope is load-bearing in pipelines 2, 3, and 6. A reader using the everyday 'extent' sense reads the scope pipeline as mere topic-narrowing and misses that scope is itself a phenomenologically grounded pattern that fixes which 'causes' and which 'deniability' tests are even admissible for a claim.

terms.doc_sense: 'When a phenomena often follows another' — an asymmetric, temporal succession-regularity between phenomena.
terms.standard_sense: A symmetric statistical association (two variables co-vary), with no built-in temporal direction. 'A regularly follows B' is succession or regularity, not correlation.
terms.misread_risk: High. Causality is defined as exceptionless correlation, so a reader importing the symmetric statistical sense loses the temporal directedness that makes the doc's 'causality' resemble causation at all, and may wrongly object 'correlation isn't causation' to a framework that deliberately builds the latter from the former.

terms.doc_sense: 'When phenomena do not correlate' — i.e., neither regularly follows the other, in the doc's succession sense of correlation.
terms.standard_sense: Statistical independence: P(A and B) = P(A)P(B). Crucially, zero correlation does NOT imply independence in standard statistics.
terms.misread_risk: Moderate. A statistically literate reader will judge the definition mathematically wrong and may discount the whole ladder — but the 'error' only exists under the substituted sense; within the doc it is just the negation of the doc's own correlation.

terms.doc_sense: 'When phenomena correlate without exception' — exceptionless observed regularity, defeasible in principle by a future counterexample.
terms.standard_sense: Modal necessity: what could not have been otherwise, true in all possible worlds — categorically stronger than any observed regularity.
terms.misread_risk: Severe. Necessity feeds causality and then the final reduction ('truth = necessary ontological event...'). Reading modal necessity in makes the framework claim vastly more than it does; the doc's necessity is an empirical, exceptionless-so-far pattern, not metaphysical inevitability.

terms.doc_sense: 'Whatever is not willed — or more accurately, independent of will (including will itself, as well as whatever is not directly observed).' An 'ontological event' is any non-willed occurrence; 'event = an ontic structure' is the reality-side term of the correspondence relation. On this definition, dreams and hallucinations are ontological/real.
terms.standard_sense: Pertaining to being or existence; ontology as the inventory of what mind-independently exists. Nothing about will. (In CS, an ontology is a formal vocabulary; in Heidegger, 'ontic' contrasts with 'ontological'.)
terms.misread_risk: Severe — probably the framework's most idiosyncratic definition. A reader assuming 'ontological = about what really exists out there' will think the framework smuggles in mind-independence claims it never makes, and will find '(including will itself)' contradictory instead of seeing the point: your own will occurs to you unbidden, so it too is will-independent in the relevant sense.

terms.doc_sense: 'Necessity, within the context of ontological events' — exceptionless succession among non-willed events, plus the inference that the causal chain starts with an uncaused event.
terms.standard_sense: A productive, mechanistic, or counterfactual relation ('A brings about B'), pointedly distinguished from mere correlation.
terms.misread_risk: Severe. The doc deliberately constructs causality from exceptionless correlation. A reader silently importing production/mechanism will misread every downstream definition (intellectual causality, truth) as making mechanistic claims, and will raise 'correlation is not causation' objections that are category errors against the doc's stipulated sense.

terms.doc_sense: 'Causality, within the context of imagination/thoughts' — one thought following another without exception; experienced as discovery, not decision ('I don't decide if something results in truth or falsehood, I simply discover it'). It is the engine of inference, validity, soundness, truth, and falsehood.
terms.standard_sense: No exact standard term, but readers will map it either to 'mental causation' (philosophy of mind: how mental states cause physical events) or to 'logical entailment' (a formal relation between propositions).
terms.misread_risk: Severe. It is neither. Reading it as entailment makes 'truth = intellectual causality within undeniability' look like a category error; reading it as mental causation drags in mind-body debates the doc never touches. The doc's notion is a phenomenological event-regularity among thoughts — logic itself as something observed to happen.

terms.doc_sense: Two coordinated senses: (a) primary, ladder step 10: 'intellectual causality, within the context of undeniability' — a thought whose denial produces inconsistency given what you currently know, always relative to a context/domain (the Newtonian example); (b) note 12.3.1: correspondence of an inferential structure with the ontic structure it refers to; final reduction: 'necessary ontological [non-willed] event, that is an undeniable imagination.'
terms.standard_sense: A mind-independent property of propositions — usually correspondence with fact — not relative to any knower's current knowledge state.
terms.misread_risk: Severe — the most dangerous collision in the document. The doc's operative 'truth' is knowledge-state-relative undeniability (epistemic), so what is 'true' can change under refinement. A reader importing the standard sense will read the framework as claiming absolute or infallible truth, then find the refinement and microbial-life notes contradictory. The internal duality (undeniability vs correspondence) compounds the hazard.

terms.doc_sense: 'Where an inferential structure may or may not correspond with the ontic structure it refers to' — i.e., the property of standing in a possible correspondence relation at all; possessing this is what promotes a statement to a claim.
terms.standard_sense: The value itself — True or False — assigned to a proposition; in classical logic every statement trivially has one.
terms.misread_risk: Moderate (near-miss). Most passages survive the standard reading, but 'claim = a statement with a truth-value' only carves out the intended class (statements that refer to an ontic structure) under the doc's sense; under the standard sense the claim/statement distinction collapses because everything has a truth-value.

terms.doc_sense: 'A statement with a truth-value' (a definitional structure that refers to an ontic structure). The final reduction sharpens this: 'claim = an undeniable set of definitions and their associations (where a false claim would be a deniable one), referring to a necessary ontological event...'
terms.standard_sense: Any assertion someone puts forward — contested by default, equally a claim whether true or false.
terms.misread_risk: High. A near-miss through most of the document, but the final reduction glosses claims as undeniable-by-default with falsehood as deniability; keeping the everyday sense makes the reduction read as 'all claims are true,' which is not what the framework says.

terms.doc_sense: 'An inferential structure'; elaborated as 'a set of definitions + their associations' — a structured composite of referring units, which may or may not carry a truth-value.
terms.standard_sense: A declarative sentence expressing something true or false; in logic, a near-synonym of proposition.
terms.misread_risk: Moderate-high. Under the standard senses of 'statement' and 'definition,' the formula 'statement = set of definitions + associations' is unintelligible (definitions are themselves statements, standardly). The reader must adopt the doc's sense of 'definition' simultaneously or the meaning pipeline appears viciously circular.

terms.doc_sense: Any unit that 'references something specific' — 'encompasses concepts, terms, etc.' The atoms statements are built from, each grounded through chains of prior definitions ending in phenomenological primitives.
terms.standard_sense: A sentence-level explanatory act giving a term's meaning ('a bachelor is an unmarried man') — not the referring concept or term itself.
terms.misread_risk: High. The meaning pipeline 'claim <- cycle of (definition <- definition) <- phenomenological primitive' reads, under the standard sense, like a regress of dictionary entries and makes the framework look circular — exactly what it is built to avoid. Under the doc's sense it is a chain of referring concepts bottoming out in raw givens.

terms.doc_sense: 'A sequence of claims in an inferential structure' — merely the sequence; grounded/valid/sound are separate optional properties. In pipeline 4, 'proof' is the external signs/support ('I feel wet... rain is occurring') observable by anyone — i.e., evidence, not derivation.
terms.standard_sense: A conclusive deductive derivation (mathematics/logic) whose existence guarantees the conclusion; everyday 'proof' also connotes decisive establishment.
terms.misread_risk: High. A reader importing the conclusive sense assumes every 'proof' in the framework certifies its conclusion; in the doc a proof can be ungrounded, invalid, and unsound and still be a proof. The external-evidence use in pipeline 4 vs the claim-sequence use in the definitions is an additional internal wobble the reader must track.

terms.doc_sense: 'When the link between a proof's conclusion and its previous steps occurs by intellectual causality' — a property of the final link only.
terms.standard_sense: A property of the entire argument: it is impossible for all premises to be true and the conclusion false; every step matters.
terms.misread_risk: Severe. The doc's valid/sound pair is shifted one notch from the standard pair: what logicians call 'valid' (every step good) is the doc's 'sound,' and the doc's 'valid' (last link good) has no standard name. Silent substitution corrupts every sentence using either word.

terms.doc_sense: 'When every link in a proof occurs by intellectual causality' — all inferential steps are good; says nothing about premises being true.
terms.standard_sense: Valid AND all premises actually true — the premise-truth condition is the entire point of the term.
terms.misread_risk: Severe. The doc's 'sound' is roughly the standard 'valid.' A reader will assume a 'sound' proof has true premises; in the doc, premise quality is handled separately by 'grounded.' The three-way grounded/valid/sound partition is invisible under standard usage.

terms.doc_sense: 'When a proof's first step is phenomenological' — the chain bottoms out in a raw given. This is the anti-circularity requirement.
terms.standard_sense: Colloquially 'well-founded, based in reality'; in metaphysics, grounding is a dependence relation between facts; in logic, groundedness of semantics.
terms.misread_risk: Moderate (near-miss). The colloquial reading ('based on good reasons') is close enough to pass unnoticed while missing the precise criterion — specifically the FIRST step must be a phenomenological primitive — which is what does the anti-regress work.

terms.doc_sense: Explicitly defined against the ordinary sense: 'whether or not denying it results in an inconsistency/knowing you're wrong... not the ability to openly deny something.' Relative to current knowledge ('based on what you know now'), and applied per scope layer — it can legitimately operate at the statistical/probabilistic level, as in the microbial-life walkthrough.
terms.standard_sense: 'Deniability' evokes plausible deniability — the social/legal ability to deny involvement. 'Undeniable' means obviously and indisputably true to anyone.
terms.misread_risk: Severe — the author anticipates this one. Deniability drives the entire truth pipeline and both final reductions. Under the plausible-deniability reading, pipeline 6 is gibberish; under the everyday 'undeniable = self-evident' reading, the framework appears to claim only obvious things are true, missing the knowledge-relative, layer-by-layer inconsistency test.

terms.doc_sense: Two coordinated senses: non-correspondence of inferential with ontic structure (12.3.2), and 'intellectual causality, within the context of deniability' — a thought whose denial is forced given what you know.
terms.standard_sense: Simply the property of being false; a false statement.
terms.misread_risk: Moderate. Parallel to 'truth': the reader misses that falsehood is knowledge-relative and produced by the same discovered intellectual-causality mechanism, rather than being a bare semantic value.

terms.doc_sense: Comprehensibility = imaginability regardless of observed context ('pink elephants' are imaginable even though elephants aren't pink); its positive form is coherence, negative is incoherence. Grounded in the limits of imagination, not in observed reality.
terms.standard_sense: Coherence = logical consistency, the hanging-together of a set of statements (cf. coherence theory of truth); incoherent = self-contradictory or unintelligible.
terms.misread_risk: High. The doc splits statement-evaluation into two axes — imaginability (coherence) vs fit-with-reality-precedent (rationality) — that standard usage merges into one notion of consistency. Hearing 'coherent = logically consistent' collapses the two levels the doc carefully separates.

terms.doc_sense: A property of statements/definitions: comprehensible within their real-world contexts — 'a pink elephant is irrational because elephants aren't pink.' Grounded in precedent taken from reality; revisable via refinement.
terms.standard_sense: A property of agents, beliefs, or reasoning processes — conforming to reason. 'Irrational' suggests fallacious or unhinged; a pink elephant would standardly be called unrealistic or contrary to fact, never irrational.
terms.misread_risk: High. Readers will hear accusations of bad reasoning where the doc only means 'conflicts with observed regularities,' and will miss that rationality here is an empirical-fit property of statement content, explicitly revisable by new evidence.

terms.doc_sense: The recursive chains inside each pipeline ('cycle of (definition <- definition)', 'cycle of (cause <- cause)') — iterated regresses that must and do terminate in something outside themselves ('all cycles must originate from something that isn't the thing itself').
terms.standard_sense: A closed loop that returns to its starting point; in graph theory and logic, precisely the structure that does NOT terminate.
terms.misread_risk: High. Under the standard sense, 'cycle of definitions' means circular definition — the exact fallacy the framework exists to avoid — so this one word, misread, inverts the framework's central move. The doc means a terminating chain.

terms.doc_sense: An induced empirical law: every kind of thing is observed to originate from something that is not that kind (chicken from non-chicken, life from non-life, universe from non-universe; deductions from inductions, observations from phenomena). It licenses the termini of all chains: the uncaused first event and the phenomenological primitive.
terms.standard_sense: Readers will assume the informal norm against circular reasoning / begging the question in arguments.
terms.misread_risk: High. The standard rule is a norm about argument form; the doc's law is an inductive generalization about origins doing heavy metaphysical lifting. Substituting the fallacy-rule sense hides the strongest (and most load-bearing) inferential lever in the framework.

terms.doc_sense: Anything that 'points to' a claim in the proof pipeline — external, publicly observable indicators (rain droplets pointing to 'I am wet'), deliberately separated from the rules of inference that connect them (held in pipeline 5).
terms.standard_sense: Semiotic sign (signifier/signified) or the casual 'indication'; 'support' as generic evidence.
terms.misread_risk: Low-moderate (near-miss). The everyday 'indicator' reading mostly works, but a semiotics-aware reader may import signifier/signified structure, and any reader may miss the deliberate separation of signs (pipeline 4) from inference rules (pipeline 5).

terms.doc_sense: Pipeline 1's output: 'what the claim is talking about, like what to imagine' — imaginative content assembled from definition-chains grounded in phenomenological primitives.
terms.standard_sense: Semantic meaning as truth-conditions, sense and reference, or use.
terms.misread_risk: Moderate (near-miss). Truth-conditions belong to the doc's ontology and truth pipelines, not the meaning pipeline; importing truth-conditional semantics merges pipelines 1, 3, and 6 that the framework insists on keeping distinct.

terms.doc_sense: The entire domain of thoughts/mental representation — the medium in which intellectual causality operates; hence 'truth = ... an undeniable imagination.'
terms.standard_sense: The faculty of forming mental images, strongly connoting fiction, fancy, and the unreal.
terms.misread_risk: High. 'Truth is an undeniable imagination' sounds like 'truth is made up' under the standard connotation. The doc means: truth is a thought-event whose denial is blocked, referring to a non-willed event.

terms.doc_sense: Generalized to any question about the intrinsic nature of something (causality, energy, dark energy, reality itself): 'hard problems are just synonyms for limits of knowledge,' present in every framework including physicalism.
terms.standard_sense: THE hard problem of consciousness (Chalmers): specifically why physical processing is accompanied by subjective experience.
terms.misread_risk: Moderate. A reader keeping the consciousness-specific sense reads note 6 as being only about consciousness debates; the doc's parity argument requires the generalized sense (every view has hard problems, so they cannot be selectively fatal to rivals).

terms.doc_sense: 'Reality' = everything not willed / independent of will — so dreams, hallucinations, and illusions ARE real (non-willed occurrences), merely categorized differently within reality. The doc explicitly diagnoses standard usage as semantic drift between a 'universal' sense and a 'not-a-dream / what everyone corroborates' sense.
terms.standard_sense: Real = existing objectively and mind-independently, explicitly contrasted with illusions, dreams, and hallucinations.
terms.misread_risk: Severe. 'Illusions are real' is flatly false in the standard sense and a theorem in the doc's sense. The entire anti-hyperskeptical argument in note 6 depends on the doc's sense; a silent substitution makes it read as self-refuting.

terms.doc_sense: A metric-driven preference procedure for going beyond direct observation: 'by some metric X, we will discover if we prefer A or B' — with the explicit norms that the metric must be identified, that 'believing requires seeing' is not an admissible default metric, and that returning the prior state of ignorance as the outcome is a misuse.
terms.standard_sense: Inference to the best explanation: generating and choosing the hypothesis that best explains the available evidence.
terms.misread_risk: Low-moderate (near-miss). Roughly compatible, but the standard reading misses the doc's specific normative bite — name the metric, and never let 'we can't know' count as the abductive conclusion.

terms.doc_sense: In the chain Observation -> Definition -> Induction -> Deduction -> Refinement: induction = 'identify/observe (assume?) the pattern behind the defined scopes'; deduction = 'apply observational precedent to patterns' and/or 'observe what occurs after intellectual causality occurs.'
terms.standard_sense: Induction = generalizing from instances to rules; deduction = deriving what necessarily follows from premises, an a priori operation independent of observation.
terms.misread_risk: Moderate. The doc recasts deduction itself as a species of observation (watching intellectual causality happen), consistent with 'I don't decide... I discover it.' A reader with the formal sense misses that in this framework even logic is phenomenologically grounded rather than stipulated.

terms.doc_sense: A defined technical property: 'a communicative structure may or may not correspond with the inferential/ontic structures it refers to' — the communication-layer analogue of truth-value, and the target of pipeline 7.
terms.standard_sense: Loose everyday fidelity: a faithful translation or retelling.
terms.misread_risk: Low (near-miss). The everyday sense points the right way but misses that faithfulness is the third layer of a precise three-layer correspondence scheme (communicative / inferential / ontic) parallel to truth.

terms.doc_sense: A type of quality that occurs phenomenologically (ladder rung 4), and the pivot for 'ontological': notably, will itself counts as ontological because it is independent of will — you do not will your willing — which is why intellectual events can have ontological causes 'even your own will.'
terms.standard_sense: The faculty of volition and choice, entangled with free-will debates.
terms.misread_risk: Moderate. The parenthetical '(including will itself)' is incoherent under the faculty sense but crucial under the doc's sense; missing it breaks the definitions of ontological, causality, and intellectual causality that stack on top of it.

terms.doc_sense: 'If you see an apple, then you objectively saw an apple' — the seeing-event is an indubitable given; whether a 'real' apple exists is a separate categorization/interpretation problem.
terms.standard_sense: Objective = mind-independent, observer-invariant fact about the external world.
terms.misread_risk: Moderate. Under the standard sense the sentence asserts the apple's mind-independent existence — exactly the claim the doc is withholding. The doc's 'objective' attaches to the occurrence of the experience, not to its interpretation.

terms.doc_sense: Pipeline 7's operation: word choice and selection tailored to audience knowledge, disposition, and language so the claim is communicated faithfully.
terms.standard_sense: Removing mystique or debunking — explaining away something that seemed mysterious.
terms.misread_risk: Low (near-miss). The debunking connotation is absent; the doc means audience-adapted wording. Mild confusion only, localized to the communication pipeline.
